title: Exploring Generative AI assisted feedback writing for students’ written responses to a physics conceptual question with prompt engineering and few-shot learning
extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether GPT-3.5 can serve as an assistant for generating feedback on students’ written responses to a conceptual physics question. The problem motivating the study is that grading open-ended responses and writing personalized feedback is time-consuming, particularly in large-enrollment introductory physics courses. The authors ask whether prompt engineering and few-shot learning can make GPT-3.5 capable of producing feedback that is correct, useful, and efficient enough to reduce instructor workload.

The intervention involved using GPT-3.5-turbo in completion mode through Azure OpenAI Studio to generate feedback on one introductory physics conceptual question about forces on two boxes. In stage 1, the authors manually categorized 20 student responses, wrote human feedback for them, and used 4 response-feedback pairs as few-shot examples in the prompt. They iteratively refined the prompt using domain-specific context and known student misconceptions. In stage 2, four student researchers compared GPT-generated and human-written feedback on 16 responses, rating each for correctness, usefulness, and whether they believed it was AI-generated. In stage 3, GPT generated feedback for 65 additional responses, and four instructors rated how much editing would be required before the feedback could be given to students.

The study took place in an introductory studio-format physics course at the University of Central Florida in the United States. The course enrolled 99 students, and 85 student written responses were collected from the class. Additional participants included four student researchers (three undergraduates and one first-year graduate student) who evaluated feedback quality, and four instructors (including two paper authors and two non-PER faculty) who judged editing needs. The context was a single conceptual physics tutorial question rather than a broad course-wide deployment across multiple assignments.

The main findings were that student raters generally saw GPT-generated and human-written feedback as similarly correct, but all four student raters tended to judge GPT feedback as more useful. Students were often poor at identifying which feedback had been generated by AI. Instructor ratings suggested that about 68% to 78% of GPT-generated feedback required only minor or no modification, with an average rating indicating minor edits were typically sufficient. The authors conclude that generative AI shows promise as a grading assistant for open-response questions when combined with prompt engineering and few-shot prompting, though they emphasize the need for human review and note important limitations in scale, generalizability, and scope.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's GPT-family large language model used here to generate natural-language feedback on students' written responses.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper used GPT-3.5-turbo via Azure OpenAI Studio in completion mode, with prompt engineering and few-shot prompting, to draft feedback on introductory physics students' written conceptual responses; outputs were compared with human-written feedback and rated by student researchers and instructors.

findings.finding_summary: In Stage 2, four student researchers rated GPT-generated and human-written feedback on 16 student responses. The authors report no clear overall trend favoring either source on perceived correctness: three of four student researchers viewed GPT-generated and human-written feedback as roughly equally correct, while one graduate student favored human-written feedback more. The paper does not report inferential statistics or effect sizes.
findings.measure: Student researcher ratings of perceived correctness of GPT-generated versus human-written feedback on 16 physics-response feedback pairs

findings.finding_summary: In Stage 2, all four student researchers tended to rate GPT-generated feedback as more useful than human-written feedback across 16 responses. The authors attribute this to GPT feedback being generally longer and more responsive to the specific student answer; five GPT-generated feedback instances were unanimously rated as more useful, while only one human-written instance was unanimously rated as more useful. No effect sizes or significance tests were reported.
findings.measure: Student researcher ratings of perceived usefulness of GPT-generated versus human-written feedback

findings.finding_summary: Student researchers had low success in identifying which feedback was AI-generated. Correct identification rates ranged from 13% to 63% across the four raters: Student A 31% (5/16), Student B 63% (10/16), Student C 13% (2/16), and Student D 19% (3/16), which the authors interpret as suggesting GPT feedback often appeared human-like at first glance.
findings.measure: Accuracy of student researchers in identifying GPT-generated feedback

findings.finding_summary: In Stage 3, four instructors rated 65 GPT-generated feedback statements on how much editing they would need before sending to students, using a 0-3 scale. Approximately 68% to 78% of feedback statements were rated as needing only minor or no modification, and the mean rating across all four instructors was 2.06 out of 3, suggesting that on average the feedback required only minor edits.
findings.measure: Instructor ratings of editing/modification needed for GPT-generated feedback (0-3 scale)

quality_tier_rationale: This is an exploratory mixed-methods evaluation with small samples (4 student raters, 4 instructors) and no randomized comparison of student learning outcomes or inferential statistics. It provides useful primary evidence on perceived feedback quality and editing burden, but not strong causal evidence of effectiveness on learning.
impact_tier_rationale: Findings suggest promising but unclear impact: GPT-generated feedback was perceived as more useful and often required only minor instructor edits, but no standardized learning gains or effect sizes were reported. Overall impact is operationally positive yet not quantified in a way that supports a higher tier.
